title: Introduction to the Ebrahim-Farrington Goodness-of-Fit Test
text: Goodness--fit testing crucial logistic regression assess whether fitted model adequately describes data. commonly used test Hosmer-Lemeshow test, several limitations: Limited power detecting certain types model misspecification Dependency grouping strategy can affect results Poor performance sparse data continuous covariates Ebrahim-Farrington test addresses limitations using modified Pearson chi-square statistic based Farrington’s (1996) theoretical framework, simplified practical implementation binary data.

code: set.seed(2026)  power_paired <- function(n, beta_quad = 0.15, n_sims = 200, G = 10) {   have_rs <- requireNamespace("ResourceSelection", quietly = TRUE)   rej <- c(EF = 0, HL = 0)   for (i in seq_len(n_sims)) {     x    <- runif(n, -2, 2)     y    <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(x + beta_quad * x^2))     fit  <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial())      # misspecified: no quadratic term     p    <- fitted(fit)      # both tests see this same dataset     if (ef.gof(y, p, G = G)$p_value < 0.05) rej["EF"] <- rej["EF"] + 1     if (have_rs &&         ResourceSelection::hoslem.test(y, p, g = G)$p.value < 0.05) rej["HL"] <- rej["HL"] + 1   }   c(n = n, EF = unname(rej["EF"]) / n_sims,     HL = if (have_rs) unname(rej["HL"]) / n_sims else NA_real_) }  power_results <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, lapply(c(200, 500, 1000), power_paired))) print(power_results, row.names = FALSE) #>     n    EF    HL #>   200 0.070 0.065 #>   500 0.165 0.155 #>  1000 0.275 0.275

what: Pros and cons of partition-based tests
title: Goodness-of-fit and calibration tests for logistic regression
text: Pros - Intuitive — compare observed vs expected event counts within groups. - Work sparse data continuous covariates, classical Pearson deviance chi-square tests break (need replicated covariate patterns). - Widely used understood (Hosmer–Lemeshow de-facto standard). - Flexible — group fitted probability (HL, EF, Pigeon–Heyse, DEF) covariate space (Tsiatis, Xie) target different kinds misfit. Cons - result depends grouping choice — number groups G grouping rule. Hosmer–Lemeshow particular known give different answers different G across software. - Limited power departures — omnibus partition tests (HL) spread degrees freedom thinly; fitted-probability grouping can miss misfit cancels along predicted probability; covariate-clustering tests can miss smooth link departures. - chi-square reference asymptotic needs adequate group sizes. DEF built fix power cons without giving size control: keeps intuitive fitted-probability grouping directs test calibration-curve shapes, ensemble removes basis choice combining directions — tops table staying nominal size. Setup: covariate x ~ Uniform(-3, 3), models fitted glm(y ~ x); tests computed one call package’s run..gof(). dashed red line marks nominal 0.05 size.

code: # Function to simulate misspecified model simulate_power <- function(n, beta_quad = 0.1, n_sims = 100) {   rejections <- 0      for (i in 1:n_sims) {     x <- runif(n, -2, 2)     # True model has quadratic term     linpred_true <- 0 + x + beta_quad * x^2     prob_true <- plogis(linpred_true)     y <- rbinom(n, 1, prob_true)          # Fit misspecified linear model     model_mis <- glm(y ~ x, family = binomial())     pred_probs <- fitted(model_mis)          # Test goodness of fit     test_result <- ef.gof(y, pred_probs, G = 10)          if (test_result$p_value < 0.05) {       rejections <- rejections + 1     }   }      return(rejections / n_sims) }  # Calculate power for different sample sizes power_results <- data.frame(   n = c(100, 200, 500, 1000),   power = sapply(c(100, 200, 500, 1000), simulate_power) ) print(power_results)

text: Grouped vs sparse forms. Pearson, Deviance   McCullagh reported two forms: default (sparse / one-trial)   form "(grouped)" form computed distinct covariate   patterns (Binomial\((m_g, P_g)\)). two identical every   covariate pattern unique (fully sparse data, simulation)   differ patterns repeat (\(m_g > 1\)). avoid clutter,   "(grouped)" row shown actually differs   sparse form (.e., pattern repeats); fully sparse data   duplicate omitted. Osius-Rojek always computed covariate   patterns, matching classical (LogisticDx) definition. Farrington vs EF. original Farrington (1996) test   grouped (covariate-pattern) test. Ebrahim-Farrington (EF) test   sparse-data counterpart: group covariate pattern   forms G data-dependent bins predicted risk, applies   directly fully sparse data. Use EF sparse binary data;   grouped Farrington form appropriate covariate patterns repeat. Reproducibility parallel path. parallel = TRUE   cluster's random-number streams initialized   clusterSetRNGStream, seeded deterministically   session's current RNG state. Two runs   set.seed state (ncores) therefore give   identical bootstrap p-values. Note parallel L'Ecuyer-CMRG streams   necessarily differ serial RNG stream, parallel = TRUE   results differ (within Monte-Carlo error) parallel = FALSE   results seed; standard valid. Results also   depend ncores, replicates split across workers.
